### Figure1
TITLE: Figure 1: Overview of the multicentre design (Fig. 1)
LEGEND:
Overview of the multicentre design. Top: the three contributing cohorts, namely, Santiago (Chile), Bilbao (Spain) and Nagoya (Japan), together with the acquisition modality of each, i.e., resting electrocardiography, finger photoplethysmography acquired during functional magnetic resonance imaging, and a 24-h wearable chest-strap recording, respectively. Bottom: the analytical contrast drawn in this work, in which the interbeat-interval series is summarized either by A) conventional linear variability indices, or by B) multiscale entropy, whereby the series is progressively coarse-grained and sample entropy is evaluated at each scale, thereby characterizing the organization of the fluctuations across temporal scales rather than their magnitude alone.
END

### Figure2
TITLE: Figure 2: Signal archetypes and conventional HRV context by cohort (Fig. 2)
LEGEND:
Signal archetypes and conventional HRV context by cohort. (A–C) Interbeat-interval traces of the analysed participants in each cohort, plotted faintly with the group mean overlaid (CETRAM, first 5 min; Cruces, whole record; Nagoya, the full 24-h record of the 47 participants analysed in the 18:00–22:00 window). (D–F) Mean heart rate by group (Nagoya: 18:00–22:00 window), shown as violin plots with individual participants overlaid; PD have higher rates in all three cohorts, significantly so only in Nagoya. (G–I) Age by group, with no cohort showing a significant difference. (J–L) Poincaré plots of successive interval pairs for one representative participant per group (the one closest to the group mean interval), with ellipses of $\pm2$ SD1 and $\pm2$ SD2, illustrating how the dispersion and the short-term correlation structure of the interval series differ across acquisition modality. All $p$ values are Mann–Whitney $U$.
END

TITLE: Figure 4: (A–D) Mean rcMSE curves with standard-error bands by group, for CETRAM, Cruces, the Nagoya 07:00–11:00 contrast window and the pre-specified Nagoya 18:00–22:00 window; shading marks the scale range entering the complexity index for that cohort, as set by the $N/\tau\geq200$ reliability rule; values beyond it are shown for context only (Fig. 3)
LEGEND:
(A–D) Mean rcMSE curves with standard-error bands by group, for CETRAM, Cruces, the Nagoya 07:00–11:00 contrast window and the pre-specified Nagoya 18:00–22:00 window; shading marks the scale range entering the complexity index for that cohort, as set by the $N/\tau\geq200$ reliability rule; values beyond it are shown for context only. In CETRAM and Nagoya entropy rises with scale over the designated range, in CETRAM only when the R apex is located correctly (Section ?); in Cruces it falls from $\tau=1$ to $\tau\approx3$–$4$ in both groups (Section ?). (E–H) Unnormalized complexity index (nAUC) by group for the same four datasets, shown as box plots giving median and interquartile range with individual participants overlaid; the upper annotation gives the unadjusted Mann–Whitney $p$ value and the lower annotation the $p$ value and AUC with mean heart rate entered as a covariate, which is the appropriate adjustment (Section ? and Supplementary Fig. S1), with HC3 standard errors. CETRAM: $p=0.031$, HR-adjusted $p=0.031$, HR-adjusted AUC 0.646. Cruces: $p=0.057$, HR-adjusted $p=0.062$, HR-adjusted AUC 0.605. Nagoya 18:00–22:00: $p<0.001$, HR-adjusted $p<0.001$, HR-adjusted AUC 0.811. The Cruces contrast points in the same direction but does not reach significance.

### Figure6
TITLE: Figure 6: Complexity index against age, by group, for each cohort and window, namely, CETRAM, Cruces, the Nagoya 07:00–11:00 contrast window and the pre-specified Nagoya 18:00–22:00 window (Fig. 4)
LEGEND:
Complexity index against age, by group, for each cohort and window, namely, CETRAM, Cruces, the Nagoya 07:00–11:00 contrast window and the pre-specified Nagoya 18:00–22:00 window. Lines are ordinary least-squares fits with 95\% confidence bands, and the annotations give the Spearman $\rho$ of the complexity index (nAUC) with age, computed within group, together with its $p$ value. Seven of the eight within-group correlations are not significant; the exception is the Nagoya 18:00–22:00 PD group ($\rho=-0.48$, $p=0.01$), which does not survive correction for the eight tests performed. The group differences reported elsewhere therefore do not appear generally attributable to the age difference between groups, although the heart-rate-adjusted models of Table ? are the more direct control.
END

### Appendix6
TITLE: Appendix 6: Discrimination and split-half reliability across the two free parameters of sample entropy, namely, the tolerance multiplier $k$ in $r=k \sigma_x$ and the embedding dimension $m$ (Fig. 5)
LEGEND:
Discrimination and split-half reliability across the two free parameters of sample entropy, namely, the tolerance multiplier $k$ in $r=k \sigma_x$ and the embedding dimension $m$. (A–B) AUC and split-half reliability against $k$, with $m=2$ drawn bold and $m=1$ and $m=3$ faint. Both are flat, in that across $k=0.125$–$0.50$ and $m=1$–$3$ the AUC moves by at most 0.061 in CETRAM, 0.076 in Cruces and 0.040 in Nagoya. Red rings mark settings at which the estimator is undefined for more than 1\% of a cohort. (C–D) AUC and reliability against $m$ at $k=0.2$. Discrimination is nearly indifferent to $m$, whereas reliability falls at $m=3$ in the two short cohorts, because longer templates match more rarely, and is flat in $m$ in Nagoya, so that $m=2$ sits at or near the reliability maximum. (E–G) AUC over the full $(k,m)$ grid per cohort, with the adopted setting boxed and cells where the estimator is undefined for more than 1\% of subjects marked by a red cross. The low-$k$, high-$m$ corner fails badly, i.e., at $k=0.05$ and $m=3$ the estimator is undefined for 90.4\% of Cruces and 55.1\% of CETRAM participants, which is the reason $k$ is not pushed below 0.125. (H) Summary of the adopted values and of the range across the usable grid. Parameters were fixed a priori by convention and were not optimized on the outcome; the per-cohort optima at $m=2$ disagree in any case, at $k=0.125$, 0.25 and 0.15 respectively. All values are nAUC over scales 1–5, in Nagoya over the full 18:00–22:00 window, where $k=0.2$, $m=2$ reproduces the primary value at those scales (AUC 0.842). A fixed absolute tolerance was considered and rejected, since it correlates with the interval standard deviation at $\rho=+0.47$ to $+0.93$ and leaves CETRAM at or near chance, i.e., it measures amplitude rather than complexity.
END

### Figure3
TITLE: Figure 3: Recording length determines which HRV marker is applicable (Fig. 7)
LEGEND:
Recording length determines which HRV marker is applicable. All panels derive from the Nagoya cohort, which is the source cohort of Suzuki et al.\ [ref], so that the minimum-SDNN values shown are a reproduction of that published analysis in the same participants. No window, scale or parameter in this figure was selected on the group contrast. (A) Complexity index in consecutive non-overlapping 15-min windows across the day, as group mean with standard-error band by clock hour; the pre-specified 18:00–22:00 window is shaded. (B) Discrimination by clock hour for complexity and for SDNN, where coverage varies by hour because recordings began in the afternoon or evening. (C) All 24 candidate four-hour windows, with filled symbols surviving Bonferroni correction across the 24 tests and both the previously selected 16:00–20:00 and the pre-specified 18:00–22:00 windows marked; the latter discriminates less well (0.815 versus 0.859), which is itself evidence that it was not selected on the outcome. (D) Discrimination of the minimum-across-day statistic against the length of the window over which that minimum is taken within the 24-h record, for both markers; the abscissa is window length and not recording duration, so that approximately 92 windows per participant remain available at the 15-min point. The shaded region marks window lengths at which $N/\tau<200$ and complexity is therefore not estimable. (E) The four distributional summaries used by Suzuki et al., namely, minimum, first decile, first quartile and median across the recording, computed for SDNN in 100-beat windows and for complexity in 15-min windows. (F) Cross-cohort comparison of minimum SDNN against complexity, in Nagoya, in the analysed CETRAM sample and in CETRAM after additionally excluding the three retained recordings with SDNN above 100 ms (Section ?). (G) Scale-resolved sample entropy to $\tau=60$ in the pre-specified window, plotted against physiological timescale and shaded by frequency band. (H) Discrimination against timescale, which peaks at $\tau=3$, i.e., approximately 2.5 s at the cohort mean interval. (I) Effect of window overlap, recomputed from the raw interval series on a sliding grid rather than by resampling the consecutive windows, and expressed relative to non-overlapping windows: raising overlap from 0\% to 90\% increases the number of windows per participant from 92 to 911 and lowers the median minimum monotonically, because the minimum over more draws is mechanically smaller, degrading the AUC of the minimum, whereas the tenth percentile and the median are unaffected.
END

Relationship between the complexity index and conventional HRV indices, in the analysed samples (CETRAM 69, Cruces 52, Nagoya 47; Nagoya indices from the 18:00–22:00 window). (A) Spearman correlation between the complexity index and conventional time- and frequency-domain indices, by cohort and group and pooled, with Benjamini–Hochberg control of the false discovery rate. (B) Cross-dataset consistency of selected correlations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals. (C) Spearman correlation of per-scale entropy with each index, by cohort; scales beyond the reliable range are greyed. (D) McFadden $R^2$ commonality decomposition of group membership into the components unique to the complexity index, unique to pNN50, unique to age and sex, and shared. (E) Pooled correlations before and after adjustment for age and sex. (F) Raw and adjusted correlations and the variance unique to each index. (G) Per-scale correlation with selected indices in Nagoya and CETRAM. The correlations use raw entropy rather than any heart-rate-normalized index. Absolute entropy values are not comparable across cohorts, because $r=0.2 \sigma_x$ makes the tolerance depend upon the low-frequency content of each recording (Section ?), so that the pooled panels use within-cohort standardized values.
END

### Figure8
TITLE: Figure 8: Exploratory associations between the complexity index and clinical measures in the 25 CETRAM PD participants with matched clinical records (Fig. 9)
LEGEND:
Exploratory associations between the complexity index and clinical measures in the 25 CETRAM PD participants with matched clinical records. (A) Raw Spearman $\rho$ between complexity, RMSSD and DFA $\alpha_1$ and the clinical variables. (B) The same correlations adjusted for age. (C–F) Scatter plots for CISI-PD total, Hoehn–Yahr stage, disease duration and CISI-PD cognitive score. (G–H) Complexity by Hoehn–Yahr stage and by non-motor symptom presence, where the box plots show median and interquartile range with individual participants overlaid. No association survived Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the false discovery rate, and the analysis is reported as exploratory rather than as evidence of a clinical correlate. (I–J) Complexity against levodopa-equivalent daily dose (LEDD) in the 21 participants with a recorded regimen, unadjusted and adjusted for disease duration. Participants were recorded on their usual medication and the time of the last dose is unknown. The underlying clinical workbook is not redistributed; see the data-availability statement.
END

Heart-rate normalization, tested and rejected. (A) Mean HR by group and cohort. (B) Correlation of the index with HR before and after dividing; division increases the dependence in every cohort. ### Appendix4
TITLE: Appendix 4: Spectral characterization and the beat-indexed time base, computed on the analysed series (CETRAM 69, Cruces 52, Nagoya 47, 18:00–22:00) (Supplementary Fig. S2)
LEGEND:
Spectral characterization and the beat-indexed time base, computed on the analysed series (CETRAM 69, Cruces 52, Nagoya 47, 18:00–22:00). (A, B) Spectral exponent $\beta$ in the beat domain (median 1.44, 1.24 and 0.61); none of the cohorts is white noise. (C) The exponent is steeper when the series is indexed by time. (D) Entropy of the real series against $1/f^{\beta}$ noise matched on length, exponent and standard deviation. In the two short resting cohorts the real and matched curves are close, i.e., their entropy is largely accounted for by the power-law spectrum, whereas the 24-h series is far less entropic than its matched noise (median excess of the noise over $\tau=1$–10, 194\%), consistent with deterministic structure, such as circadian, postural and activity-related changes, that a stationary power law does not reproduce. There is no group difference in $\beta$ in any cohort ($p=0.21$–$0.99$): PD alters the amplitude of the complexity measure, not the spectral exponent. Because an interval series is indexed by beat rather than sampled at a fixed rate, coarse-graining at $\tau$ spans $\tau\times$ mean RR seconds and the physical timescale differs between groups wherever heart rate does.
END

### Appendix7
TITLE: Appendix 7: The Cruces cohort in the context of the source study (Supplementary Fig. S3)
LEGEND:
The Cruces cohort in the context of the source study. (a) Discrimination, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals, for the complete resting HRV metric set of Iniguez et al.\ [ref] recomputed in the same 52 participants, together with our complexity index (outlined). (b) The corresponding Mann–Whitney $p$ values on a logarithmic axis. RMSSD, SD1 and HF power attain nominal $p<0.05$, none after correction for the ten metrics, and NNiqr, which the source study selected as its primary metric on the basis of its heart–brain synchronization maps, is not among them. (c) For comparison, the clinical autonomic findings reported in that paper, plotted on their own axis; these values are quoted from the publication and were not recomputed here, since we did not have access to the autonomic-test or neuroimaging data. Collectively, the panels indicate that the PD group is clinically dysautonomic while its resting interbeat-interval series separates the groups only weakly, and that the complexity index behaves like the conventional measures in this cohort.
END

### Appendix3
TITLE: Appendix 3: Sensitivity of the complexity index to analysed recording length (Supplementary Fig. S4)
LEGEND:
Sensitivity of the complexity index to analysed recording length. Each participant's interval series is truncated to a common number of beats, so that changes reflect length rather than cohort composition; each cohort is restricted to the participants present at all of its ladder points. Discrimination and split-half reliability both rise with length in Nagoya, the only cohort whose recordings permit the full ladder.
END

### Appendix2
TITLE: Appendix 2: Per-scale discrimination across acquisition contexts (Supplementary Fig. S5)
LEGEND:
Per-scale discrimination across acquisition contexts. In CETRAM, scale $\tau=1$ yields the largest group separation; in the Nagoya 18:00–22:00 window separation is nearly flat over $\tau=1$–6 (AUC 0.83–0.84, peak at $\tau=3$) and declines slowly thereafter. In the photoplethysmographic cohort, interbeat intervals are derived from the maximum upstroke slope of the pulse wave; separation is similar to that in CETRAM at $\tau=1$–$4$ (AUC 0.64–0.67) and disappears at $\tau=5$, the scale at which the Cruces entropy curves turn and at which its records reach the reliability limit (Section ?). Shaded regions mark scales that fail the $N/\tau\geq200$ reliability rule.
END

### Validation
TITLE: Validation: Methodological validation of the entropy implementation, in the 69 analysed CETRAM recordings (Supplementary Fig. S8)
LEGEND:
Methodological validation of the entropy implementation, in the 69 analysed CETRAM recordings. (A) Reference processes of known complexity (white noise, $1/f$ noise, an AR(1) process, the logistic map and a periodic signal with noise), analysed with the same code and fixed tolerance as the cohort data, with the CETRAM group-mean curves overlaid. (B) Sensitivity of the index to spurious long intervals injected into real recordings. (C) Discrimination over entropy type (sample, fuzzy), $m$ and $k$. (D) Choice of complexity index (sample entropy at $\tau=1$, nAUC over 1–3, 1–5, 1–10 and 1–20, and slope), unnormalized and divided by heart rate, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals. (E) Discrimination of nAUC(1–$k$) against the upper scale $k$. (F) Discrimination against analysed length in the 50 recordings with at least 1000 beats (unnormalized index). (G) The unnormalized index against heart rate, and the change that division by heart rate induces in the correlations with conventional indices. The ratio is shown for comparison only; it was not adopted (Methods). This is a methods figure and not a results figure.
